claims.text: High-entropy alloy nanoparticles contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios.
The nanoparticles initially form a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution with minimal chemical ordering.
Above approximately 1500 K, increased thermal energy enhances atomic diffusion in the nanoparticles.
In a reactive catalytic ambient, selective oxidation or gas interactions lower local bonding stability.
Reactive-gas-induced loss of local bonding stability triggers surface segregation and incipient phase separation.
In an inert atmosphere, high configurational entropy and lattice distortion maintain a homogeneous solid-solution structure.
Higher configurational entropy can stabilize solid-solution phases, with its stabilizing contribution increasing with temperature.
Lattice distortion enhances the stability of a single-phase solid solution relative to phase separation or ordering.
Atomic-size disparities within approximately 15% are a relevant Hume–Rothery condition for stable substitutional solid solutions.
The applicability of the 15% atomic-size rule to high-entropy alloys is established sufficiently to define the hypothesis boundary.
Reactive gas interactions lower effective diffusion barriers for selected elements at high temperature.
Lower diffusion barriers promote selective oxidation, local chemical ordering, and elemental segregation.
Suppressing oxidation in an inert atmosphere allows entropy and lattice distortion to preserve the uniform solid-solution phase.
Above approximately 1500 K, reactive conditions will produce detectable surface segregation, minor secondary phases, or local chemical ordering.
Under inert conditions up to 1923 K, the nanoparticles will retain a single-phase structure with only minor lattice distortions.
In situ high-temperature XRD and TEM/EDS can be used to compare phase evolution and elemental segregation under reactive and inert atmospheres.
Very small nanoparticle size or strong support interactions may alter the predicted stability behavior.
The segregation-onset temperature and extent of chemical ordering depend on the metal combination and nanoparticle size.
A lack of detectable differences in segregation, ordering, or secondary-phase formation between reactive and inert environments would falsify the hypothesis.
